title: How to Read a Chinese Calendar: Grid, Solar Terms, Almanac
description: Chinese calendar: 42 Monday-start cells, no lunar day in grey cells, one badge per cell (holiday first), Five Elements by year stem, holidays end 2026-10-10.
content:
The site's Chinese calendar puts three things on one screen: a 42-cell month grid, the list of solar terms in the current month, and an almanac panel on the right. Reading it means keeping track of which day and which year each of the three takes its values from — the lunar day in a cell, the lunar year in the header, and the sexagenary cycle and Five Elements in the panel do not always rest on the same basis.

1. Three anchors on load: month title, lunar-year header, almanac panel

Top left is a month title such as “November 2026”, and the small line beneath it is the lunar-year header, “Lunar Year 2026 · Bing-wu horse year”; top right are Previous month, Today and Next month, in that order; the right column is a card that reads values day by day. The three anchors have different bases: the month title decides which month the cells lay out, the lunar-year header is decided by the 1st of the month alone, and the panel follows the selected day exactly.

No button press is needed to open the page: at module top level the script sets viewYear, viewMonth and selected to today's local date, then calls render() once, which draws the header, the grid, the solar-term row and the panel together. The default selected cell carries both the gradient circle that means today and the outline that means selected.

PositionWhich day it readsOn 2026-11-10 at load
Month title #calMonthThe year and month being browsedNovember 2026
Lunar-year header #calLunarYearThe lunar date of the 1st of the monthLunar Year 2026 · Bing-wu horse year
Solar Terms This Month #calTermsEvery day of the month, queried once eachStart of Winter (7) / Minor Snow (22)
Almanac panel #almanacThe selected dayNovember 10 / lunar month 10, day 2 · day of Wu-zi

2. 42 cells starting on Monday: why grey cells have no lunar day

The grid is always 42 cells, 7 columns by 6 rows, whether the month has 28 days or 31. The offset of the first cell comes from (first.getDay() + 6) % 7: JS numbers Sunday as 0, and the formula shifts that to Monday as 0, so when the 1st falls on a Sunday the offset is 6. November 1, 2026 is a Sunday, so the first 6 cells are October 26 to 31, November 1 lands in the “Sun” column, and 6 cells of December 1 to 6 are appended at the end; February 1, 2026 is also a Sunday, with the first 6 cells being January 26 to 31 and 8 cells of March 1 to 8 appended.

These leading and trailing cells carry the other-month class and 0.3 opacity. Their lunar-day text is emptied: the template writes ${isCurrent ? lunar.getDayInChinese() : ''}, so only days inside the month get a label such as “day one” or “day twenty-one”. A grey cell keeps nothing but the Gregorian number — do not read it as a lunar day.

  • A grey cell only omits the lunar day; the badge still renders: the October 2026 view appends November 1 to 8, so the Start of Winter badge for November 7 sits in a grey cell, and the February view appends March 1 to 8, so the Awakening of Insects badge for March 5 sits in one too.
  • Trailing cells reach 14 at most, which happens only in a February whose 1st is a Monday; between 2020 and 2040 that means February 2021, February 2027 and February 2038, and the last two rows are then entirely next month.
  • Clicking a grey cell does not change the month: a click only swaps selected for the cell's data-y/m/d and calls render() again, leaving the view year and month alone. In the February 2026 view, clicking January 26 keeps the header at “February 2026” and switches the right column to “January 26 · lunar month 12, day 8 · day of Geng-zi”, with the outline landing on that translucent grey cell.

3. One badge per cell at most: a holiday beats a solar term

A badge is the small rounded label under the day number, and the code is a single ternary: holiday ? { text: holiday.getName(), cls: 'holiday' } : jieQi ? { text: jieQi, cls: '' } : null. Each cell gets at most one, so a day that is both a holiday and a solar term draws the holiday only, in the red error colour, while a solar-term badge uses the theme colour.

Four days in 2026 fall on that crossing: February 18 (Spring Festival and Rain Water), April 5 (Qingming Festival and Qingming), May 5 (Labour Day and Start of Summer), and June 21 (Dragon Boat Festival and Summer Solstice). In the grid those four days read “Spring Festival”, “Qingming Festival”, “Labour Day” and “Dragon Boat Festival”.

The solar term has not disappeared, it has moved: the “Solar Terms This Month” row still lists “Rain Water (18)”, and the panel for that day shows two tags at once, “Spring Festival (Holiday)” and “Rain Water”, one red and one in the theme colour. To tell whether a day has a solar term, do not look only at the cell.

4. “Solar Terms This Month” is a list for the month, not a countdown

The bottom row scans getJieQi() for every day of the browsed month and joins the hits into chips such as Start of Winter (7), with the term name first and the day of the month in parentheses. November 2026 gives “Start of Winter (7)” and “Minor Snow (22)”; December gives “Major Snow (7)” and “Winter Solstice (22)”; February gives “Start of Spring (4)” and “Rain Water (18)”. It covers only the month currently in view, changes as you page through months, and never shows how many days are left until the next term.

All 2,412 months between 1900 and 2100 contain exactly two solar terms, so the fallback line “No solar terms this month” is never actually seen; the Good for and Avoid fallbacks “Nothing special to recommend” and “Nothing special to avoid” did not fire in 2024 to 2026 either. They are code branches, not an interface state you can expect.

Solar-term dates have to be computed per month rather than written as constants: the observatory's definition splits the 360-degree ecliptic into 24 equal parts of 15 degrees of longitude, with the spring equinox at 0 degrees and Start of Winter at 225 degrees, tracking the sun's position, which is why every render scans the month again.

5. The right panel: one day's numbers come from two calendars

Top to bottom, the panel shows the Gregorian date with its weekday, the lunar date, a holiday or solar-term tag, two columns of Good for and Avoid chips, and four blocks of metadata. It mixes two sources: the date, the weekday and the star sign come from the Gregorian calendar, while the lunar month and day, the sexagenary cycle and the zodiac come from the lunar one.

The block most easily misread is “Five Elements”. It is computed as wuxing[ganZhi.charAt(0)], where ganZhi is getYearInGanZhi() — the year pillar — so the block holds the element of the year stem, not of the day stem. November 10, 2026 is a Bing-wu year and a Wu-zi day: Bing maps to Fire and Wu to Earth, and the panel reads “Fire”. On February 1 the year pillar is Yi-si and the element block reads “Wood”; only when the year changes to Bing-wu on February 17 does it become “Fire”.

“Year (Ganzhi)” need not agree with the header either: the panel takes the selected day, the header takes the 1st of the month. In the February 2026 view, after selecting the 17th, the header still reads the Yi-si snake year while the panel already shows “Zodiac Horse / Year (Ganzhi) Bing-wu year / Five Elements Fire”.

The Good for and Avoid columns are the string arrays returned by lunar-javascript's getDayYi() and getDayJi(); the page only renders them as chips. November 10, 2026 has 17 Good for entries (marriage, consecration, travel … putting on mourning dress) and 2 Avoid entries (property purchase, installing a bed); February 17 has 10 Good for and 2 Avoid (marriage, moving into a house). These are library data, not advice offered by this tool or this article.

6. The header's lunar year comes from the 1st of the month

That header line is built from Solar.fromYmd(viewYear, viewMonth, 1).getLunar(), so it takes the lunar year of the 1st of the month. The consequence is clearest in February 2026: February 1 is still the twelfth month of the Yi-si year, so the header reads “Lunar Year 2025 · Yi-si snake year”, and although 2026-02-17 is already the first day of the first lunar month, the header stays on Yi-si for the whole month; only March switches it to “Lunar Year 2026 · Bing-wu horse year”.

The year boundary is worth remembering too: the year pillar and the zodiac change at the first day of the first lunar month, not at the Start of Spring. Start of Spring falls on February 4, 2026, and that day is still Yi-si; only February 17 turns it into Bing-wu and Horse. In a month that straddles the Spring Festival, it pays to read the header and the panel together.

7. Holiday data stops at 2026-10-10

Holiday names in the badges come from HolidayUtil.getHoliday(ymd). A day-by-day scan (1990 to 2035) returns 860 days: the first is 2001-12-29 (New Year's Day, a make-up workday) and the last is 2026-10-10 (National Day, a make-up workday). Within 2026 alone there are 39 days: 33 days off plus 6 make-up workdays, covering 7 names — New Year's Day, Spring Festival, Qingming Festival, Labour Day, Dragon Boat Festival, National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival.

After October 10 there is not a single record: for November 2026, December 2026 and the whole of 2027, getHoliday() returns null every time. So the November 2026 grid has no holiday badge at all, only the two solar-term badges for Start of Winter and Minor Snow, and in the December grid, besides this month's Major Snow and Winter Solstice, the grey cells appended at the end also carry Minor Cold on 2027-01-05. This is not “November has no holidays”; it is “the library has not recorded them yet”.

The other tool does say it out loud: the working days calculator checks getHolidays(year) year by year and, when data is missing, shows “Holiday data is missing for these years; only weekday rules apply” together with the years. The Chinese calendar page has no such line — missing data simply means no badge.

8. Navigation, keyboard and Today

The three controls behave differently: Previous month and Next month change only viewYear and viewMonth and call render(), leaving the selected day alone, so after paging the right column still shows the old day; the Today button resets the view and the selected day together. Crossing a year works: from December 2026, Next month gives January 2027, and from January 2026, Previous month gives December 2025. The arrow keys are bound on window and behave like clicking Previous month and Next month.

“Today” has two layers: the default view and default selected day come from the new Date() evaluated when the page loads, while the button reads the clock again inside its click handler. Pin the fake clock to 2026-11-10T03:00:00Z and the page opens on November 10; push the clock to 2026-12-20 and click Today, and the view jumps to December with the 20th selected — it reads the moment of the click.

It reads local time as well: at the same instant 2026-11-10T20:00:00Z, a browser in UTC defaults to November 10 while a browser in Asia/Shanghai defaults to November 11 (it is already 04:00 there), so aligning “today” across time zones starts with naming the time zone.

9. Boundaries and limits: treat it as a lookup tool

  • Three bases on one screen: the month title decides which month the cells show, the lunar-year header looks only at the 1st of the month, and the panel looks only at the selected day — a month that straddles the Spring Festival is the easiest to misread.
  • Grey cells drop the lunar day but keep a valid badge; do not judge a solar term from the cell alone, because a holiday badge covers it.
  • Holiday data runs from 2001-12-29 to 2026-10-10; before and after that range (including all of 2027) there is no data, and the page does not flag the gap.
  • Make-up workdays also carry the red holiday badge (2026-10-10 does); only the panel's tag tells “(Holiday)” from “(Workday)”.
  • The Five Elements block is the year stem's element, not the day stem's; the year-pillar block and the header may not even be the same year.
  • Good for and Avoid are strings returned by lunar-javascript; the page neither explains nor sorts them.
  • Leap months show up only in the panel: 2025-07-25 is the first day of the leap sixth month, and the right column reads “lunar leap month 6, day 1 · day of Yi-wei” while the cell shows only “day one”.

To get the conversion itself straight, use the Gregorian–lunar converter; to count the days between two dates, the date difference calculator; to look up a zodiac sign by date, the zodiac lookup; and if you only care about working days and make-up shifts, the working days calculator. This article describes how this page behaves across 70 browser assertions and 21 Node checks; it makes no claim about choosing auspicious dates or about fortune.

faqs.q: How do I read a day's lunar date and sexagenary cycle on the Chinese calendar?
faqs.a: Click that day in the month grid and the right panel's first line switches to the Gregorian date and weekday, the second line to “lunar month 10, day 2 · day of Wu-zi”, the third to a holiday or solar-term tag, and the last four blocks to zodiac, star sign, year pillar and Five Elements. The panel follows only the selected day and is independent of the year and month shown in the header.

faqs.q: Why do some cells show only a number and no lunar day?
faqs.a: The grid is fixed at 42 cells and is padded with the neighbouring months whenever the month does not fill it; those cells carry the other-month class and 0.3 opacity, and their lunar-day text is emptied (the template is isCurrent ? getDayInChinese() : empty string). A grey cell therefore keeps only the Gregorian number, but badges inside it stay valid — for example the Awakening of Insects badge on March 5 at the end of the February 2026 view.

faqs.q: Why can't I see a Rain Water badge during the Spring Festival?
faqs.a: Each cell has room for one badge only, and the code gives the holiday priority over the solar term, so a day that is both draws the holiday. Four days in 2026 do this: February 18 (Spring Festival and Rain Water), April 5 (Qingming Festival and Qingming), May 5 (Labour Day and Start of Summer) and June 21 (Dragon Boat Festival and Summer Solstice). The solar term still appears in the “Solar Terms This Month” row and as a tag in the panel.

faqs.q: The header says Yi-si snake year but the panel says Bing-wu and Horse — which is right?
faqs.a: They read different days. The header takes the lunar year of the 1st of the month, so the whole of February 2026 reads “Lunar Year 2025 · Yi-si snake year”; the panel takes the selected day, and 2026-02-17 is the first day of the first lunar month, already Bing-wu and Horse. For a day inside the month trust the panel; for the month title trust the header.

faqs.q: Why does November 2026 have no holiday badge at all?
faqs.a: Holiday data comes from HolidayUtil.getHoliday(), and the range measured in this round runs from 2001-12-29 to 2026-10-10, 860 days in total; after 2026-10-11 (all of 2027 included) it returns null. November, December and 2027 therefore carry no holiday badge, and the page gives no warning about the missing data — check the official holiday schedule separately.

faqs.q: Is the “Five Elements” block the element of the day stem?
faqs.a: No. The code is wuxing[first character of the year pillar], that is the year stem's element. November 10, 2026 is a Bing-wu year and a Wu-zi day: Bing is Fire and Wu is Earth, and the panel reads “Fire”. So within one lunar year the block never changes; it switches only with the year.

focus: The Chinese calendar puts a 42-cell month grid, the month's solar-term list and an almanac panel on one screen, with three different bases: cells and the header go by the 1st of the month, the panel by the selected day; grey cells drop the lunar day but keep their badge; each cell holds one badge and a holiday beats a solar term; the Five Elements block takes the year stem, not the day stem; and holiday data stops at 2026-10-10, after which there are no badges and no warning.
